opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the most pervasive problems in education, and it connects to something I care about a lot from the developmental side. Goodhart's law says that once a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. In schools, we started out with tests that were meant to be rough indicators of whether children were learning, and then we turned those indicators into the thing itself. So now you have teachers teaching to the test, schools optimizing for scores, and parents optimizing for grades and résumés, and the actual learning, the exploring and understanding, gets squeezed out.

What makes this especially striking from my perspective is that if you look at how young children actually learn, it's almost the opposite of that kind of target-driven optimization. Children are wonderful explorers. They're like the research and development division of the human species. They try lots of things, many of them apparently pointless, they play, they ask "why" endlessly, and that broad, high-variance exploration is exactly what lets them build rich models of the world. That kind of learning is really hard to measure. You can't easily put a number on "this child has developed a flexible, causal understanding of how things work."

So what happens is that schools, partly for good reasons like accountability, focus on the things that are easy to measure: can you produce the right answer on this particular kind of problem? And the system gets very good at producing that. Kids become very good at a sort of narrow exploitation, figuring out what the teacher wants, what the test wants. But you lose the exploratory part. In some of our experiments, when you instruct children directly, "here's how this toy works," they'll do exactly that and stop exploring, whereas if you let them discover, they find out much more about the toy. Schooling at scale can have that same effect.

And I'd say it shows up even more dramatically at the top end, in the competition for elite colleges. You get these extraordinarily accomplished teenagers who have optimized every metric, grades, test scores, extracurriculars, and many of them are anxious and somewhat brittle, because they've been trained to hit targets rather than to be curious. The irony is that the qualities we actually want, creativity, resilience, the ability to deal with genuinely new problems, are precisely the things that get undermined when you optimize too hard for the measures.

I don't think the answer is to get rid of measurement entirely. But I think we need to recognize that the most important things about learning, especially for younger children, are things that resist being turned into targets. And sometimes the best thing we can do is to give children a safe, rich environment and then, to some extent, get out of the way.

r001.rationale: The response says students can become skilled at optimizing for grades and tests while losing curiosity, creativity, and resilience. It does not state that being good at school becomes a distinct skill that stops tracking the broad abilities it is meant to predict in adulthood.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's actually one of the most important things to understand about why schools are the way they are, and why they so often seem to be at odds with what we know about how children actually learn.

So Goodhart's law, of course, is the idea that once a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. And school is almost a textbook case. We started out wanting children to be curious, to understand things, to be able to think flexibly about the world. Then we said, well, how do we know whether that's happening? Let's test them. And the tests were, at first, a reasonable proxy. But the minute the tests became the thing that mattered — for the kids, for the teachers, for the principals, for the real estate values in the district — the whole system reorganized itself around the test rather than around the learning.

And what's striking from a developmental point of view is how much that's in tension with the way children are designed to learn. The thing that children do best, from the time they're babies, is explore. They're incredibly good at figuring out how the world works through play, through trying things out, through asking questions that nobody has told them to ask. That kind of exploration is, almost by definition, not something you can target. If you tell a child exactly what to find, they'll find it, but they'll stop looking at everything else. There's actually nice experimental work on this — when an adult explicitly teaches a child what a toy does, the child learns that one thing and explores less than a child who's just handed the toy.

So school, in a sense, is a machine for turning exploration into exploitation. It takes this broad, messy, high-variance search that children are so good at and narrows it down to a very specific set of outcomes that you can measure. And of course there are good reasons for that. Reading and arithmetic really do need to be learned, and there are some things you really do have to practice in a focused way. I don't want to be romantic about it. But I think we've drifted much too far toward the measurable end, especially for younger children.

The other thing I'd say is that Goodhart's law has a kind of developmental twist here, because the people being measured are also the people whose motivational systems are being shaped. If you spend ten or twelve years in an environment where what counts is the score, you don't just get kids who are good at tests. You get kids who have learned that the point of learning is the score. And then you see what we're seeing now in a lot of elite universities — extremely capable students who are very anxious, very risk-averse, very good at figuring out what the professor wants and much less interested in figuring out what's actually true. That's Goodhart's law operating on the person, not just on the institution.

I think the honest answer is that we probably can't escape this entirely. Any large system has to measure something. But we could at least be more humble about it, and leave more room — especially in early childhood — for the kind of learning that doesn't show up on any test but that turns out to matter most in the long run.

r001.rationale: The response says schools can train students to focus on scores and tests, but it does not state that being good at school becomes a distinct skill that stops tracking broader abilities expected to predict adult outcomes.

astra-6.text:
I think education is a particularly good example, because what we actually want is for children to understand things, to be curious, to be able to figure out something they haven’t encountered before. Those are very difficult things to measure. So we find something that we can measure, like how well they do on a test, and then we organize the whole system around improving that measure.

The problem isn’t that tests tell you nothing. It’s that being good at taking the test can come apart from the capacities you were trying to assess. If you spend your time practicing exactly the kinds of problems that will appear on the test, your scores may improve without your understanding becoming much deeper.

And there’s a particular irony with children, because exploration often looks inefficient. You try things that don’t work. You get distracted by something interesting. You ask a question that takes you away from the lesson. But those can be precisely the activities that lead to deeper learning. If every activity has to produce a measurable improvement right away, you risk squeezing out the very things that make children such powerful learners.

r001.rationale: The response says test-taking skill can separate from the understanding tests aim to assess, but it does not state that being good at school becomes a distinct skill that stops tracking broad abilities meant to predict adult performance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think education is a very good example of the problem. What you actually want is for children to understand the world, to be curious, to be able to figure out something they haven’t encountered before. But those things are difficult to measure. So you find something that you can measure, like performance on a standardized test, and then organize the institution around improving that performance.

The trouble is that children are very good at learning what you’re asking them to do. If what you’re asking is, “Figure out what answer the teacher wants,” they’ll learn to do that. But that’s a different activity from asking, “How does this actually work?” You can end up rewarding behaviors that look like learning while discouraging the exploration that makes learning possible.

That doesn’t mean you shouldn’t assess children or care whether they can read. Of course you should. It means that a measure that’s useful as one source of information can become much less useful when it becomes the purpose of the whole enterprise.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes test performance and learning to give the teacher’s expected answer from broader understanding and exploration, but it does not say that being good at school becomes a separate skill that stops tracking abilities meant to predict adult performance.
